meta.title: Who really said "Houston, we've had a problem"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: This version is the real one. NASA's transcript has it verbatim — but Jack Swigert said it first, not Jim Lovell. "We have a problem" is the movie's rewrite.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Houston, we've had a problem'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified in the Apollo 13 Flight Journal's corrected air-to-ground transcript, 13 April 1970. Jack Swigert transmitted it first; Lovell repeated it. The 1995 film changed the tense.

answer.label: Spoken first by
answer.authorDates: 1931–1982 · NASA astronaut; command module pilot, Apollo 13
answer.sourceLine: This one is real — it is the other version that is wrong. At 055:55:19 mission elapsed time on 13 April 1970, command module pilot Jack Swigert transmitted “Okay, Houston… we’ve had a problem here,” and after CAPCOM Jack Lousma asked the crew to say again, commander Jim Lovell repeated it in the exact familiar five words — “Ah, Houston, we’ve had a problem” — both preserved verbatim in the Apollo 13 Flight Journal ↗. The present-tense “Houston, we have a problem” that people often “correct” this to is dialogue written for Ron Howard’s 1995 film, which Wikiquote ↗ records as an alteration of what was actually said.

source.excerpt:
055:55:19 Swigert: Okay, Houston…
055:55:19 Lovell: …Houston…
055:55:20 Swigert: …we’ve had a problem here. [Pause.]
055:55:28 Lousma: This is Houston. Say again, please.
055:55:35 Lovell: [Garble.] Ah, Houston, we’ve had a problem. We’ve had a Main B Bus Undervolt.
trail: 13 April 1970 — the transmission. The Apollo 13 Flight Journal ↗, whose page for this moment is titled “Houston, we’ve had a problem”, logs Swigert at 055:55:19–20 GET (“Okay, Houston… we’ve had a problem here”), Lousma at 055:55:28 (“This is Houston. Say again, please”), and Lovell at 055:55:35 (“Ah, Houston, we’ve had a problem. We’ve had a Main B Bus Undervolt”).

The primary record — and the correction to it. NASA’s contemporaneous Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription ↗, held on the NASA Technical Reports Server (“Work of the US Gov. Public Use Permitted.”), logs the exchange at 02 07 55 19–35 elapsed — but it assigns the first call to the LMP and the CDR, and renders it “I believe we’ve had a problem here.” The speaker identifications and the exact wording used on this page follow the Flight Journal’s corrected transcript, and NASA’s own history article credits the call to Swigert.

NASA still writes it this way. The agency’s own history article, “Houston, We’ve Had a Problem” ↗, uses the past-perfect wording in its title and body, places the crew “some 205,000 miles from Earth”, and states that the warning lights “prompted Swigert to call Mission Control”.

Where the other version came from. Wikiquote’s sourced page for the 1995 film ↗ notes that “in real life, the quote was ‘Houston, we’ve had a problem’”, that the original phrase was pronounced by Swigert and repeated by Lovell, and that it “was altered to a present-tense in the film script”.
source.excerptNote: Timestamps are Ground Elapsed Time, and the two men briefly talk over each other. Note that Swigert reaches the words first, and that both use the past perfect — “we’ve had”. The oxygen tank had exploded moments earlier; the Main B Bus Undervolt was the symptom on the panel in front of them. Mission Control’s internal loop traffic between 055:55:26 and 055:55:30 — GUIDO and FLIGHT, talking to each other rather than to the spacecraft — is omitted, so this is an air-to-ground extract rather than an unbroken run.
source.rightsNote: The sentence was spoken over a NASA radio link by a NASA astronaut on a NASA mission, and NASA’s contemporaneous transcript of the loop ↗ is catalogued on the NASA Technical Reports Server with the explicit statement “Work of the US Gov. Public Use Permitted.” Works of the United States federal government carry no copyright, so this wording is free to quote despite its 1970 date. The rewritten movie line, “Houston, we have a problem”, is a different matter: that one is 1995 screenplay dialogue and remains in copyright.

author.name: Jack Swigert
author.kicker: The man who actually called it in
author.heading: Jack Swigert — the late addition who made the call
author.metaLine: 1931–1982 · NASA astronaut; command module pilot, Apollo 13
author.bio: John L. “Jack” Swigert Jr. was not supposed to be aboard Apollo 13 at all. He flew on the backup crew until three days before launch, when he replaced Ken Mattingly — the prime crew had been exposed to German measles and Mattingly lacked immunity, so NASA declined to risk him. Three days into the flight, Swigert became the first human being to report the accident that crippled the spacecraft. He later left the astronaut corps and, on 2 November 1982, was elected to represent Colorado’s 6th congressional district with 64% of the vote; he died of respiratory failure on 27 December 1982, aged 51, after treatment for cancer, and never took his seat.

cite.sourceCitation: W. David Woods, Johannes Kemppanen, Alexander Turhanov, Lennox J. Waugh and William Smeaton, eds., “Day 3, part 2: ‘Houston, we’ve had a problem’,” Apollo 13 Flight Journal, 055:55:19–055:55:35 GET (corrected transcript). The contemporaneous Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription (Houston: NASA, 1970), NASA Technical Reports Server document 20160014370, logs the first call to the LMP and the CDR. The present-tense variant “Houston, we have a problem” originates in Apollo 13, directed by Ron Howard, screenplay by William Broyles Jr. and Al Reinert (Imagine Entertainment / Universal Pictures, 1995).

copyAttribution: "Okay, Houston… we've had a problem here." — Jack Swigert, command module pilot, Apollo 13, transmitted at 055:55:19 mission elapsed time on 13 April 1970 and repeated seconds later by commander Jim Lovell as "Ah, Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt." Recorded in the Apollo 13 Flight Journal's corrected air-to-ground transcript; Swigert credited by NASA's own accident history. The familiar "Houston, we have a problem" is the 1995 film's rewrite, not the transmission.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about the version that is right
misattribution.intro: This is an inverted misquote. The wording most people think is the mistake is the authentic one, and the wording they think is authentic came out of a screenplay. What genuinely needs correcting here is the speaker.

items.who: Jim Lovell, who usually gets sole credit
items.why: Lovell did say it — “Ah, Houston, we’ve had a problem” at 055:55:35 GET — but only after CAPCOM Jack Lousma asked the crew to repeat. The first transmission was Swigert’s, at 055:55:19. Lovell said so himself in his chapter of NASA’s 1975 Apollo Expeditions to the Moon: “Jack Swigert saw a warning light that accompanied the bang, and said, ‘Houston, we’ve had a problem here.’ I came on and told the ground that it was a main B bus undervolt” — quoted here ↗, which also credits Swigert as the one who coined the phrase.

items.who: Apollo 13 (1995), screenplay by William Broyles Jr. and Al Reinert
items.why: Anyone who tells you the line is really “Houston, we have a problem” is quoting Tom Hanks, not the spacecraft. Wikiquote’s page for the film ↗ states outright that in real life the quote was “Houston, we’ve had a problem” and that the phrase “was altered to a present-tense in the film script”. Broyles explained the change as a matter of drama, not accuracy.

items.who: The 1974 television drama Houston, We’ve Got a Problem — and NASA itself in 1983
items.why: The film was not first. Wikipedia records that the 1974 TV drama Houston, We’ve Got a Problem “had brought a misstatement of the phrase into popular culture years earlier”, and that in 1983 NASA used the now-current misquotation “Houston, we have a problem” as the title of its weekly radio programme about space history — both documented here ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: What actually crossed the gap between Apollo 13 and Houston on 13 April 1970 was: “Okay, Houston… we’ve had a problem here” (Swigert, 055:55:19 GET), then “Ah, Houston, we’ve had a problem. We’ve had a Main B Bus Undervolt” (Lovell, 055:55:35 GET) — both in the past perfect, both preserved verbatim in the Apollo 13 Flight Journal ↗.

context.heading: The famous misquote runs the other way
lead: On the third day of the flight, with Apollo 13 some 205,000 miles from Earth, the crew had just finished a television broadcast when an oxygen tank in the service module exploded. What went out over the radio was not a cry of alarm but clipped engineering shorthand: something had happened, and here was the symptom. As NASA’s own account ↗ puts it, the Master Alarm and the Main DC B Bus Undervolt light came on a second or two after the bang, which prompted Swigert to call Mission Control. Lovell later fixed the moment at 21:08 hours on 13 April.

The past perfect was accurate. It was also, dramatically speaking, inert — and that is exactly why the 1995 film changed it. Screenwriter William Broyles Jr. explained the swap in terms quoted by Wikipedia ↗ from a 2017 Washington Post piece: the real line “is saying something has happened, and it’s over. The past perfect tense wasn’t as dramatic as ‘We have a problem’ — which meant that the problem was happening right then and was continuing, which in fact it was and would shortly cause the mission to abort.” He was right about the drama. The rewritten line ranked No. 50 on AFI’s 100 Greatest Movie Quotes in June 2005 — as a movie quote, which is exactly what it is.
context.detailsSummary: Why the drift is stubborn — and older than the film
detailsBody: The film usually takes the blame, but it inherited the problem. Wikipedia notes that although the Houston Chronicle later identified Ron Howard’s 1995 film as the source of the popular misquotation, “the error was of longer standing”: the 1974 television drama Houston, We’ve Got a Problem had already put a mangled version into circulation, and in 1983 NASA itself used “Houston, we have a problem” as the title of its weekly radio programme about space history.

By 1995 the wrong version was so entrenched that the film was, in effect, quoting the audience back to itself. The Apollo 13 Flight Journal makes the same point — Howard’s film used the misquote because by then it was what viewers expected to hear.
The result is an unusual trap: someone who knows the line “properly” from the movie will confidently correct a person who has just quoted it accurately.
context.pull: The tense was the whole point. “We’ve had” is a report. “We have” is a crisis.

sourcesVerified.claim: The transcript records Swigert at 055:55:19-20 GET saying "Okay, Houston... we've had a problem here", Lousma at 055:55:28 saying "This is Houston. Say again, please", and Lovell at 055:55:35 saying "[Garble.] Ah, Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt." The page is titled "A13FJ - Day 3, part 2: 'Houston, we've had a problem'" and comments that the legendary line delivered by Lovell is the past-perfect one, not the familiar present-tense version popularised by the Tom Hanks movie.

NASA's own history article is titled "Houston, We've Had a Problem", places the crew "some 205,000 miles from Earth", and states the warning lights "prompted Swigert to call Mission Control, 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.'" followed by Lousma's "Say again, please" and Lovell's reply adding the Main B Bus Undervolt detail.

The NTRS record for the Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription (NASA, document 20160014370) carries the rights statement "Work of the US Gov. Public Use Permitted" and public distribution status. The document itself logs the exchange as "02 07 55 19  LMP  Okay, Houston - -" / "02 07 55 20  CDR  I believe we've had a problem here." / "02 07 55 28  CC  This is Houston. Say again, please." / "02 07 55 35  CDR  Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a MAIN B BUS UNDERVOLT." — so the 1970 transcript does not assign the first call to the CMP and does not carry the familiar wording; both come from the Flight Journal's corrected transcript.

Wikiquote's Apollo 13 (film) page states: "In real life, the quote was 'Houston, we've had a problem.' The original phrase pronounced by Jack Swigert, 'Houston, we've had a problem here' and then repeated by Lovell, 'Houston, we've had a problem', was altered to a present-tense in the film script." It also credits the screenplay to William Broyles Jr. and Al Reinert and notes the AFI #50 ranking.

Wikipedia's article gives the original form as "Okay, Houston ... we've had a problem here" coined by Jack Swigert and Lovell's reply as "Ah, Houston, we've had a problem"; quotes Lovell's chapter in Apollo Expeditions to the Moon (1975) crediting Swigert and fixing the time at 21:08 on April 13; quotes Broyles that the past perfect "wasn't as dramatic as 'We have a problem'"; records the 1974 TV drama Houston, We've Got a Problem as having brought a misstatement of the phrase into popular culture years earlier; records NASA's 1983 use of the misquote as a weekly radio programme title; and gives the AFI No. 50 ranking in June 2005.
NTRS record 19760005868 is "Apollo Expeditions to the Moon", edited by E. M. Cortright, NASA SP-350, 1975, with rights statement "Work of the US Gov. Public Use Permitted."

Jack Swigert was born 30 August 1931 and died 27 December 1982 aged 51 of respiratory failure after cancer treatment; he was Apollo 13's command module pilot, assigned three days before launch replacing Ken Mattingly after German measles exposure; he was elected to Colorado's 6th congressional district on 2 November 1982 with 64% of the vote and died before taking office; and the article states he "was the astronaut who first announced" the line.
Jim Lovell was born 25 March 1928 and died 7 August 2025 aged 97; he commanded Apollo 13 and co-wrote the 1994 book Lost Moon with Jeffrey Kluger, adapted into the 1995 Ron Howard film Apollo 13.
